source: 광운대 편입영어 2019~2026학년도 기출 출제 유형(문항 수·영역·문제 꼴, VocabFactory 분석)을 분석해 dailyfreetoolbox 가 새로 만든 연습 문제

passages.text: In the eighteenth century, most shops displayed no prices; buyers and sellers haggled over every purchase, and the final sum depended on the nerve and cunning of each party. Quaker merchants broke with this custom. Convinced that asking one customer more than another was a form of lying, they set a single fixed price for every item. Rivals at first considered the policy commercially ____, yet customers came to trust it, and fixed prices gradually became the norm.

When we are calm and replete, we find it remarkably difficult to foresee how powerfully hunger, dread, or fatigue will sway our choices later. Psychologists call this blind spot the hot-cold empathy gap. Shoppers who wander through a supermarket while famished, for instance, tend to leave with far more than they intended to buy. The pragmatic lesson is to make consequential decisions in advance, while we are still ____, and to bind ourselves to them before temptation arrives.

The word muscle has a surprisingly playful origin. It comes from the Latin musculus, which meant little mouse. Ancient observers, it seems, thought that a flexing muscle, rippling beneath the skin of an arm, resembled a small mouse scurrying under a cloth. The same comparison appears elsewhere; in ancient Greek, a single word could denote both a mouse and a muscle. The term thus preserves a vivid ____ that most people who use it have long since forgotten.

Supermarkets sometimes sell a few staple items, such as milk or eggs, for less than they paid for them. These loss leaders are hardly acts of philanthropy. The store is wagering that customers enticed by the bargain will fill their carts with other merchandise that carries lucrative margins, so that the deficit on one product is more than offset by profits elsewhere. The strategy succeeds, however, only as long as shoppers ____. If they seize the discounted item and head straight for the checkout, the scheme simply backfires.

For decades, internet service from space had a dismal reputation. Conventional communication satellites sit in geostationary orbit, about 36,000 kilometers above the equator, where they orbit the planet in lockstep with its rotation and therefore appear fixed in the sky. A single satellite at that altitude can cover roughly a third of the globe, but the distance exacts a toll. Even at the speed of light, a signal needs about a quarter of a second to travel up and back, a lag that renders video calls awkward and online games almost unplayable. (A)
Low-Earth-orbit networks attack the problem by bringing the satellites much closer, typically a few hundred to about two thousand kilometers up. (B) The diminished distance trims the delay to a level comparable with many ground-based connections. (C) A satellite that low races across the sky in minutes, so an operator needs thousands of them, handing each connection from one to the next, merely to keep a single subscriber online. Such constellations were long considered prohibitively expensive to build; reusable rockets and mass-produced satellites have made them ____.
The results became conspicuous after 2022, when terminals shipped to Ukraine helped sustain communications as terrestrial networks were sabotaged or destroyed. (D) Since then the service has spread to remote farms, cargo ships, airliners, and disaster zones. (E) Critics observe, however, that a handful of private companies now control infrastructure on which governments and armed forces increasingly depend, a concentration of power that few regulators anticipated.

In 1815 the inventor Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented a device that ticked out a steady beat at whatever speed a musician selected. He was a shrewd entrepreneur, and he found an avid patron in Ludwig van Beethoven, who soon began adding precise metronome numbers to his scores. For the first time, a composer could tell performers exactly how fast he wanted a piece to move.
Musicians have been squabbling over those figures ever since. Many of Beethoven's markings are so brisk that pianists regard them as nearly impossible to execute without blurring the music. Some scholars conjecture that his metronome was defective; others propose that he read the scale on the wrong side of the sliding weight, or that, being deaf, he chose his tempos at a desk, hearing the music only in his head, where it can travel faster than fingers allow. A few performers insist that the markings mean exactly what they say and play accordingly, with dazzling results. Most, however, conclude that the numbers should be <u>taken with a grain of salt</u>: a valuable clue to the composer's intentions, but not a command to be obeyed at any cost.

"Too literal. Try again." The note, scrawled in red ink across the top of my first assignment, was the only comment Ms. Moore made on the twelve pages I had translated. A modest publishing house had hired me to render a Portuguese novel into English, and I had labored over those pages for a month, checking every word against three dictionaries. I was proud of their meticulous precision. She, evidently, was not.
For weeks I rewrote, my indignation mounting, and for weeks the pages came back bearing the same four words. I began to suspect that she harbored some personal animosity toward me. Then one evening, sorting through a box of old files she had asked me to discard, I came across a yellowed manuscript: her own first translation, completed thirty years earlier. Across its top, in faded red ink, someone had written: Too literal. Try again.
I read her pages that night and grasped what my dictionaries could never teach me. Her early sentences, like mine, were impeccable and inert; they conveyed the meaning of the Portuguese but none of its music. The next morning I did something I had never ventured to do. I shut the dictionaries, read a paragraph aloud in Portuguese, and wrote down how it ought to ____ in English rather than what it literally said. When the chapter returned a week later, there was no red ink at all, only a faint pencil mark in the margin: Better. Keep going. <u>I have kept that page on my desk ever since.</u>

For decades, many American employers have required workers to sign noncompete agreements, contracts that bar them from joining a rival or launching a competing business for a set period after they leave. They were once reserved for senior executives with access to trade secrets, but they have spread to hairstylists, warehouse staff, and fast-food employees. Critics contend that such restraints (A) ____ wages, because a worker who cannot accept a better offer down the street has little leverage to demand a raise.
In April 2024 the Federal Trade Commission voted to ban most of these agreements nationwide, estimating that roughly one in five American workers was bound by one. Business lobbies sued at once, arguing that the agency had exceeded its authority, and in August 2024 a federal judge in Texas blocked the rule before it could take effect. The struggle has since shifted to the states. California has long refused to enforce most such contracts, and several other states have restricted them for lower-paid workers. Defenders of the clauses insist that they protect investments in training and confidential knowledge; opponents reply that such interests can be guarded by (B) ____ tools, such as confidentiality agreements, that do not prevent anyone from working.

A woodpecker can strike a tree trunk thousands of times a day, hammering at speeds that would leave a human boxer senseless. For decades biologists assumed that the bird's skull must work like a shock absorber, and that spongy bone and a long, tongue-supporting bone cushioned the brain against each blow. The notion was so alluring that engineers appropriated it when designing protective helmets.
A study published in 2022 challenged this picture. Researchers filmed woodpeckers with high-speed cameras and measured how abruptly their heads slowed on impact. If the skull were absorbing shock, the head should have decelerated more gently than the beak. It did not; head and beak stopped almost simultaneously. Indeed, the team calculated, any genuine cushioning would ____ the bird, because the beak would then have to be driven harder to chisel the wood. How, then, does the brain elude injury? The answer appears to be its diminutive size. A woodpecker's brain is so small and light that the forces it endures, though formidable by human standards, remain below the level known to cause concussions in primates.

When esports appeared as a medal event at the Asian Games in Hangzhou in 2023, many older spectators were baffled. Teenagers in team jerseys sat almost motionless before screens while commentators shouted, and an arena full of fans greeted each decisive maneuver as if it were a goal. For the competitors, however, the occasion was a long-awaited vindication. Competitive gaming had grown from basement tournaments into an industry with professional leagues, salaried athletes, and audiences of millions, yet it had long been dismissed as a pastime rather than a sport.
Whether gaming deserves that label is a question older than it looks. Traditional sports bodies have generally defined sport by physical exertion, and skeptics point out that a player who scarcely leaves a chair can hardly be compared with a marathon runner. Defenders reply that elite players perform hundreds of precise actions per minute and train for many hours a day, and that shooting and archery, which also demand little visible ____, have long been Olympic events.
Sports federations have nonetheless been drawn in, partly for a pragmatic reason: their audiences are graying. Adolescent viewers devote far more time to gaming streams than to traditional broadcasts, and officials hope that esports will introduce them to the wider sporting world. In 2024 the International Olympic Committee announced plans for a separate Olympic Esports Games. The arrangement reflects a cautious compromise. Games that simulate real sports or involve abstract strategy have been welcomed, while titles built around realistic violence have been kept at arm's length, since they sit uneasily with the Olympic ideal of peace.

In 2023 Detroit unveiled the first public road in the United States that can charge electric vehicles while they are moving. Copper coils buried beneath a short stretch of pavement generate a magnetic field, which transmits energy to receivers mounted under specially equipped cars. Supporters argue that such roads could eventually let manufacturers install smaller, lighter batteries. For now, however, the technology remains ____: the pilot stretch is only about a quarter of a mile long, and few vehicles can use it.

Asked whether people in California are happier than those in the American Midwest, most respondents in both regions say yes, citing the sunshine. When researchers actually measured life satisfaction, however, they found almost no difference. The mistake, which psychologists call the focusing illusion, arises because whatever we happen to be thinking about seems more ____ than it really is. Daily happiness depends far more on work, health, and relationships than on the weather.

When something goes terribly wrong, we call it a disaster without a thought for the heavens. The word, however, comes from the Italian disastro, built from a prefix meaning bad and astro, meaning star. It reflects an old belief that the positions of the planets and stars governed human affairs, so that a calamity could be blamed on an unfavorable alignment overhead. Every disaster, in a sense, still carries a faint trace of ____ in its name.

Buy now, pay later services let shoppers split a purchase into a few interest-free installments, and their popularity has soared among young consumers. Retailers welcome them because customers who can (A) ____ payment tend to spend more. Critics warn that the sheer ease of such loans tempts people to juggle several plans at once and lose track of what they owe. Moreover, because many of these loans have not been reported to credit bureaus, other lenders may (B) ____ how much debt an applicant already carries.

Much of the security that shields online banking, e-mail, and software updates rests on a mathematical wager: that certain problems, such as finding the prime factors of an enormous number, are so laborious that no computer could solve them in any useful span of time. (A) In 1994 the mathematician Peter Shor demonstrated that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could, in principle, factor such numbers with astonishing speed. (B) No machine remotely capable of the feat yet exists, and estimates of when one might appear vary widely.
Security agencies are not waiting to find out. Their worry centers on a tactic sometimes summarized as harvest now, decrypt later. (C) An adversary could intercept and store encrypted traffic today, gambling that it can be unlocked once quantum hardware matures. Medical records, diplomatic cables, and trade secrets that must remain confidential for decades are therefore ____ already.
In August 2024, after an international competition lasting roughly eight years, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology published its first three standards for post-quantum cryptography, methods built on mathematical problems believed to withstand quantum as well as conventional attacks. (D) Governments and technology companies have begun the slow task of replacing older systems, a migration that experts compare to rewiring a city while its lights stay on. (E) Cryptographers caution that the new methods, too, rest on assumptions rather than proofs, which is why they urge organizations to design systems that can swap one algorithm for another without being rebuilt from scratch.

In 1899 the American economist Thorstein Veblen published The Theory of the Leisure Class, a biting study of how the wealthy spent their money. He argued that much of their spending was meant not to satisfy any practical need but to display status. He coined the phrase conspicuous consumption to describe purchases whose chief purpose is to be seen, from lavish banquets to servants whose only work was to look idle on their employer's behalf.
Economists later gave his name to a curious category of products. For most goods, demand falls as prices rise. For a Veblen good, a higher price can make the item more desirable, because the expense itself is part of what is being bought. Luxury watches and designer handbags are often cited as examples; a firm that cut their prices sharply might find that buyers lost interest. The idea helps explain why some brands refuse to hold sales and have even destroyed unsold stock rather than let it be sold cheaply, a practice that has drawn growing criticism. For such goods, a low price would ____ the very exclusivity that customers are paying for.

The parcel on my doormat is addressed to an H. Lindqvist, Apartment 4C. I live in 4B, and in the eight months since I moved in, I have never laid eyes on the occupant of 4C, though a radio used to murmur faintly through the wall late at night. The box is light and rattles when I tilt it. I knock on the neighboring door; nobody answers. I leave a note and carry the parcel inside, intending to return it that evening.
That evening stretches into three days. On the fourth, a frail man leaning on a cane knocks on my door, apologizing for the intrusion. He found my note, he explains, buried beneath a pile of flyers; his eyesight is failing, and he seldom ventures out since his hip operation. When I hand him the box, his face brightens. Inside, he tells me, are replacement parts for <u>his only companion</u>, which fell silent a week ago and without which his evenings have been unbearably ____.
I offer to help him install the parts, and he accepts with evident relief. His apartment is a mirror image of mine, but crammed with books in four languages. While I fumble with tiny screws, he talks about the decades he spent as a ship's engineer, sailing between Gothenburg and Busan. When the radio finally crackles back to life, he insists that I stay for coffee, and it dawns on me that I have lived beside this remarkable man for eight months without once learning his name. It seems an auspicious moment to begin.

For decades, American customs law contained a little-known provision known as the de minimis exemption, which allowed parcels worth less than a modest threshold to enter the country free of duties and with minimal paperwork. In 2016 Congress raised that threshold from 200 to 800 dollars, intending to (A) ____ trade for small businesses and travelers. The consequences were unexpected. As online platforms began shipping inexpensive clothing and gadgets directly from overseas factories to individual buyers, the number of such parcels exploded, passing a billion a year. Customs officers could inspect only a sliver of them, and domestic retailers complained that rivals were exploiting the rule to undercut them.
In 2025 the United States ended the exemption, first for goods from China and then for parcels from virtually every country, so that even cheap orders now face duties. The European Union, facing a similar flood of small packages, has moved to (B) ____ its own duty-free threshold. Bargain hunters may pay more, but governments argue that the old rule had turned a convenience into a loophole.

Few sounds are as soothing to cat owners as a purr, yet for decades scientists could not agree on how cats produce it. Most mammals vocalize by pushing air past their vocal folds, which vibrate at a pitch determined by their size and tension. A purr, however, is very low, often around twenty to thirty vibrations per second, which seemed far too low for the small vocal folds of a house cat. The prevailing explanation held that the brain must drive the muscles of the larynx to twitch rhythmically, like a drummer keeping time.
A study published in 2023 complicated that view. Researchers examined larynges from cats that had been euthanized for medical reasons and found that, when warm, humidified air was blown through them, they emitted purr-like sounds with no input from the nervous system at all. The key appears to be pads of connective tissue embedded in the vocal folds, which add mass and allow them to vibrate unusually slowly. The finding does not exclude a role for the muscles in living cats, but it suggests that anatomy itself may do much of the work. Why cats purr is another matter; they do so not only when content but also when injured or frightened, which implies that the sound is more than a simple signal of ____.

Few symbols on a keyboard have a stranger history than the ampersand. Its shape began as a ligature, a joining of the two letters of the Latin word et, meaning and. (A) Scribes writing in haste ran the e and the t together, and examples of the combined form have been found scratched on walls in Pompeii, the town buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE. Over the following centuries copyists elaborated the sign in countless ways, until in many typefaces it scarcely resembles its two parent letters at all.
The name is younger and odder still. (B) In nineteenth-century British and American schoolrooms, children reciting the alphabet were taught to finish not with Z but with the symbol, which counted as a sort of twenty-seventh letter. (C) Because it would have been confusing to say a lone and at the end of the list, pupils added the Latin phrase per se, meaning by itself: and per se and. Chanted rapidly by generations of children, the phrase was gradually ____ into a single word, ampersand.
Today the sign has been dropped from the alphabet, but not from daily life. (D) Companies favor it in their names because it suggests partnership, and type designers treat it as a chance to show off, since its form is far less fixed than that of ordinary letters. (E) Some designers even judge a whole typeface by this one character, seeing it as the clearest window onto the personality of the font.

Small Bluetooth trackers were designed to help owners retrieve misplaced keys and luggage, but they have also been exploited to stalk people surreptitiously. In 2024 Apple and Google introduced an industry standard under which phones warn users when an unfamiliar tracker appears to be traveling with them, regardless of whether the tracker or phone is made by Apple or another company. The measure is a sobering reminder that a gadget built for convenience can readily become an instrument of ____.

Confronted with two tasks, people frequently gravitate toward the one with an imminent deadline even when the alternative promises a more substantial reward. In experiments published in 2018, participants opted for tasks described as expiring shortly, despite knowing that a task with no time limit would pay more. The researchers dubbed this proclivity the mere urgency effect. Urgency, it seems, can ____ importance in our minds, which may explain why trivial e-mails so often eclipse consequential work.

The word bankrupt has a vividly physical origin. In the market squares of Renaissance Italy, moneylenders did business at wooden benches, and the Italian word for bench, banca, also gave English the word bank. According to a popular account, when a lender could no longer pay his debts, his bench was broken, and the phrase banca rotta, or broken bench, came to mean financial ruin. Whether or not benches were ever literally smashed, the term preserves the image of a livelihood ____.

The first person to acquire a telephone possessed a device of negligible value, since there was no one to call. Each new subscriber, however, rendered every existing phone more useful. Economists call this a network effect: the value of a product escalates with the number of people who use it. Network effects help explain why a handful of social media platforms and messaging apps come to monopolize their markets. Once most of your friends have joined one service, switching to a rival, however superior, means ____, so even disgruntled users tend to stay.

Most cars spend more than ninety percent of their lives parked. For a gasoline car that idleness is merely wasteful; for an electric car it may be a latent asset. A modern electric vehicle carries a battery large enough to power an average home for a day or more, and engineers have long asked whether those batteries, sitting in driveways and parking garages, could help stabilize the electricity grid. (A)
The concept is called vehicle-to-grid. A car tethered to a bidirectional charger would absorb electricity when it is cheap and plentiful, such as on sunny afternoons when solar panels create a glut of power, and relinquish some of it during the evening peak, when demand surges and prices soar. (B) Spread across millions of vehicles, such a system could act like an enormous power plant scattered across a country, reducing the need for costly backup generators that operate only a few hours a year. (C)
Coordinating it, however, requires a smart grid: a network in which meters, chargers, and utilities exchange information continuously, so that power flows can be adjusted minute by minute. (D) Pilot projects in several countries have shown that the technology works, and some electric school buses, which sit idle during summer vacations, already sell power back to utilities. Formidable obstacles remain. Many drivers fear that incessant charging and discharging will degrade their batteries, and bidirectional chargers are still expensive. (E) Unless owners are confident that their cars will be ready when they need them, and fairly paid for the service, the idea is likely to remain ____.

For roughly three centuries, European painters could buy a rich brown pigment made, quite literally, from Egyptian mummies. Ground-up human and animal remains, mixed with resin, produced a warm, translucent color that artists prized for shadows and skin tones. The ingredient did not seem as macabre to earlier generations as it sounds; powdered mummy had long been sold by apothecaries as a medicine, and its use in paint seemed a natural extension of that trade.
Attitudes changed in the nineteenth century, as public interest in ancient Egypt grew and more people learned what the pigment actually contained. According to a story told by his nephew, the writer Rudyard Kipling, the painter Edward Burne-Jones was so horrified when he discovered the source of his tube of mummy brown that he buried it in his garden. Buyers grew scarce, and in the 1960s, by one account, a London color maker announced that it had run out of mummies to grind. Today the name survives mainly as a curiosity, a reminder that the history of art materials is sometimes stranger, and ____, than the history of art itself.

Late one autumn, a family of field mice discovered an ear of corn lying at the far edge of the meadow, fallen from a farmer's cart. It held enough kernels to feed them through the winter, but its sheer heft was daunting, and dark clouds were gathering in the west.
The eldest mouse, who prided himself on his brawn, proclaimed that he alone would lug it home. He strained and heaved until his whiskers quivered, yet the ear did not budge. His brother, scoffing at such feebleness, tried next and fared no better. One by one the others took their turn, grunting and puffing, each convinced that the failure of the rest proved only their weakness, and each retiring, exhausted and ____, while the clouds crept closer.
At last the smallest mouse, whom nobody had thought to consult, spoke up. Why, she wondered, did they keep taking turns? Wouldn't the ear move more easily if everyone pushed at once? Her chastened siblings exchanged sheepish glances. They had been so intent on proving who was strongest that the idea had never occurred to them.
They arranged themselves along the length of the ear, and at a signal from the smallest, all of them pushed together. The ear trundled forward, slowly at first and then steadily, across the meadow and down into their burrow, just as the first heavy drops began to fall. That winter, whenever the eldest played the braggart, the others reminded him of the afternoon when the whole family had accomplished with ease what none of them could manage alone.

Discussing salaries has long been something of a taboo in European workplaces, and that reticence, critics argue, helps camouflage persistent disparities between what men and women are paid for comparable work. In 2023 the long-running campaign for equal pay won a victory when the European Union adopted a directive on pay transparency that member states must incorporate into national law by June 2026. Under its provisions, employers will have to state a starting salary or salary range in job advertisements or before interviews, and they may no longer ask candidates about their pay history. Employees will gain the right to request information on average pay levels, broken down by sex, for workers doing the same work or work of equal value. Larger companies must also report their gender pay gaps regularly, and where an unexplained gap of five percent or more persists, they must assess it jointly with workers' representatives.
Supporters say the rules will ____ the bargaining position of applicants, who until now have often negotiated without knowing what colleagues earn. Some employers worry about administrative burdens and about friction among staff once salaries are no longer secret.

Anyone who has gulped an icy drink on a sweltering day knows the abrupt, excruciating pain that can ensue, felt not in the mouth but behind the forehead. Doctors call it a cold-stimulus headache; most people simply call it brain freeze. The pain usually subsides within a minute, but its cause long perplexed researchers, since the brain itself has no pain receptors.
The leading explanation involves blood vessels near the roof of the mouth. When something very cold touches the palate, adjacent blood vessels are thought to constrict and then rapidly dilate as the body strives to rewarm the area, and the nerve that carries sensation from this region also serves much of the face and forehead. The brain, receiving the signal, <u>misplaces the source of the pain</u>, attributing it to the head rather than the mouth. Because the episode is fleeting and benign, it has even served as a convenient proxy for studying more debilitating headaches, such as migraines, which may involve similar changes in blood flow. The practical advice is simple: eat ice cream slowly, or press the tongue against the roof of the mouth to warm it.

For several decades, chip engineers enjoyed a lucky bargain. As transistors shrank, each one consumed proportionally less power, so a chip could pack in more of them without growing hotter. Around the mid-2000s that bargain broke down. Transistors kept shrinking, but their power consumption no longer fell in step, and the heat produced per square centimeter of silicon began to rival that of a stovetop burner. Since then, managing heat has become as (A) ____ to chip design as raw speed.
The problem has grown acute with the processors that train and run artificial intelligence models. A single high-end accelerator can draw upwards of a thousand watts, and data centers cram thousands of these voracious devices into dense racks. Fans that push air across metal fins, the method that cooled computers for generations, are approaching their limits, because air is a poor conductor of heat. Operators are therefore turning to liquids. In direct-to-chip systems, coolant flows through cold plates mounted on top of the processors; in immersion cooling, entire servers are submerged in vats of fluid that does not conduct electricity.
Liquid cooling entails its own complications, from seepage to the cost of retrofitting buildings designed for air. It also raises questions about water, since some facilities rely on evaporation to shed heat. Yet the alternative is to let chips (B) ____ themselves, deliberately slowing down to avoid overheating, which squanders much of the exorbitantly priced hardware. Some engineers believe that the next leap will come not from better cooling at all but from chips designed to produce less heat in the first place.

A: I've revised this cover letter five times, and I still can't decide whether it's polished enough to submit.
B: ____
Then you'd better start writing it at last.
Congratulations on getting the job, then.
You should have revised it at least once.
Stop second-guessing yourself and just hit send.
I'm glad you mailed it without any hesitation.
다섯 번이나 고쳐 쓰고도 보낼지 망설이는 사람에게는 '그만 의심하고 보내라(Stop second-guessing yourself)'는 말이 어울려요. 이미 다 썼으니 이제 쓰기 시작하라는 말, 한 번은 고쳤어야 한다는 말은 앞말과 어긋나요. 아직 보내지도 않았으니 합격 축하나 망설임 없이 보냈다는 말도 맞지 않아요.

Travelers who book flights at the last minute during the holidays often end up paying through the ____ for cramped seats.

pay through the nose 는 '터무니없이 비싼 값을 치르다'라는 관용구예요. 연휴 직전에 표를 사면 좁은 좌석도 비싸다는 흐름에 맞아요. by the skin of one's teeth(간신히), a pain in the neck(골칫거리), keep one's chin up(기운 내다), Achilles' heel(약점)은 pay through 와 짝을 이루지 않아요.

앞 문장은 '사람을 끌어모으다'라는 동사 draw, 뒤 문장은 '무승부'라는 명사 draw 예요. gather 는 앞 문장에만 맞고 무승부 뜻이 없어요. split·cycle·boom 은 play to a ~ 꼴로 쓰지 않아요.

• The court took a ____ stance against companies that hide fees in fine print.
• After ten years at a large law ____, she opened her own practice.

• A quiet, well-lit room is ____ to the kind of deep concentration that serious study requires.
